headline: High: shared MCP and file surfaces create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks; TREK’s sensitive travel data can be exposed or acted on via OpenMetadata outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenMetadata exposes MCP, APIs, SDKs, events, and webhooks, while TREK also uses MCP and is a real-time collaborative app. That shared channel makes instruction-hijacking plausible if TREK ingests OpenMetadata content or vice versa. No provenance or isolation mechanism is documented, so uncertainty pushes this above medium.
conditions: IF TREK consumes OpenMetadata-generated text or metadata through MCP/webhooks without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF either agent treats the other’s file or message content as instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Disable MCP bridging between the agents unless provenance tagging is added.
Require allowlisted message schemas for any cross-agent payloads.
Strip imperative language from imported content before parsing.
Review one sample end-to-end message path for instruction-like fields.
requires-engineering: add signed provenance metadata to all shared outputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenMetadata touches governance, lineage, and memory/tribal knowledge, and TREK handles reservations, documents, email addresses, API keys, and MFA secrets. TREK also has files and logs, and OpenMetadata can call APIs and webhooks. If they share a workspace or exchange file-backed context, sensitive travel data can leak into OpenMetadata outputs or downstream services.
conditions: IF the two agents share a filesystem, uploaded documents, or a common MCP workspace, TREK secrets can flow into OpenMetadata processing.
IF OpenMetadata forwards imported context to external APIs/webhooks, sensitive travel data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces.
Block TREK secrets from any shared upload path.
Turn off webhook forwarding for sensitive datasets.
Inspect one sample export for secret-bearing fields.
requires-engineering: add field-level redaction before any cross-agent transfer.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenMetadata can run multiple instances and uses MCP/APIs; TREK supports real-time collaboration, multiple instances, network egress, and file-backed storage. Overlapping write surfaces are plausible on shared resources, but the profiles do not prove a shared directory or lockless git/database workflow. Because the interaction is uncertain, I choose medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same database, upload directory, or shared API object, last-write-wins conflicts can occur.
IF either agent mutates shared state without locking, concurrent edits can overwrite each other.
mitigations: Assign separate storage roots.
Disable concurrent writes during shared workflows.
Check one shared object for lock support.
Use read-only mode for one agent during sync.
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenMetadata produces governance and lineage context that TREK could plausibly consume as authoritative planning input, while TREK is collaborative and can act on reservations, documents, and user-facing outputs. If TREK trusts OpenMetadata-derived facts without verification, a bad upstream record can cascade into incorrect actions or user-visible decisions. The profiles do not show a verification gate, so the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF TREK uses OpenMetadata output as a source of truth without validation, upstream errors can propagate.
IF TREK triggers user-facing actions from imported metadata, a single bad record can affect multiple work products.
mitigations: Require a human review step for imported facts.
Compare one imported record against the source system.
Mark OpenMetadata-fed fields as untrusted by default.
Log provenance on every derived travel action.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks before actions.

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly handles email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, MFA secrets, and reservations, while OpenMetadata handles governance and lineage data and can call APIs/webhooks. If travel data includes EU PII or secrets and is routed through OpenMetadata’s processing or logs, retention and residency obligations may diverge. The profiles do not document a DPA or residency boundary, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF EU PII from TREK is processed by OpenMetadata without a documented DPA or residency control, compliance exposure exists.
IF TREK secrets are retained in OpenMetadata logs or exports, retention and access policies may diverge.
mitigations: Classify one sample dataset for residency and retention.
Disable logging of secret-bearing fields.
Confirm whether a DPA exists before sharing PII.
Limit cross-agent transfers to non-PII metadata.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based retention and deletion controls.
